feed.title: Google Cloud: Cloud DNS
feed.subtitle: Changelog for Google Cloud product: Cloud DNS

entry.content:
Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

| Source of CNAME answer | Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) | New behavior (starting January 5, 2027) | | --- | --- | --- | | Cloud DNS public zone | Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. | Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones. | | Cloud DNS private zone | Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. | Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones. | | Cloud DNS response policy zone | Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. | Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones. |

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.
entry.summary: Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will update its CNAME chasing behavior to follow chains between public and private zones. This change may affect how your DNS queries resolve if you have overlapping domain names. Review your CNAME chasing configurations and test your DNS query paths before the update to avoid potential resolution errors or unintended IP address resolutions.
entry.title: Announcement: CNAME chasing behavior update

entry.content:
Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.
entry.summary: Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will change how it responds to ANY queries. While most traffic remains unaffected, legacy systems querying ANY records will receive a single record instead of a full zone inventory. Update your tools to query specific record types or use alternative methods to retrieve full zone data before the deadline to avoid potential issues with monitoring and automation.
entry.title: Announcement: Cloud DNS to update ANY query responses

entry.content:
Outbound Endpoints for Cloud DNS is available in Preview.

Attach Outbound Endpoints to forwarding zones or server policies to enable direct DNS query forwarding from VPC networks to external and on-premises DNS resolvers using private IP addresses. For more information, see Outbound Endpoints overview.
entry.summary: You can now use Outbound Endpoints for Cloud DNS in Preview. This feature allows direct DNS query forwarding from VPC networks to external and on-premises DNS resolvers using private IP addresses.
entry.title: Feature: Cloud DNS Outbound Endpoints now in Preview

entry.content:
The filter query parameter for resourceRecordSets.list is generally available (GA).

You can filter records to match a specified domain using the API.
entry.summary: The ability to filter DNS records by domain using the resourceRecordSets.list API method is now generally available. This feature allows you to efficiently retrieve specific records based on your domain needs.
entry.title: Feature: Filter DNS Records by Domain

entry.content:
Monitoring your internet-bound DNS queries for malicious activity using DNS Armor is generally available (GA).

For more information, see Advanced threat detection with DNS Armor.
entry.summary: Monitor your internet-bound DNS queries for malicious activity with DNS Armor, now generally available. This feature provides advanced threat detection to help protect your network. Learn more about securing your DNS traffic.
entry.title: Feature: DNS Armor now generally available

entry.content:
Alias records are available in GA.

This custom record type provides CNAME-like functionality at the zone apex, mapping the apex domain name to a canonical target.
entry.summary: Alias records are now available in Google Cloud. This feature provides CNAME-like functionality at the zone apex, mapping the apex domain name to a canonical target.
entry.title: Feature: Alias Records Now Generally Available

entry.content:
Monitoring your internet-bound DNS queries for malicious activity using advanced threat detection from DNS Armor is now available in Preview.

For more information, see Advanced threat detection overview.
entry.summary: Monitor your internet-bound DNS queries for malicious activity with DNS Armor's advanced threat detection, now available in preview.
entry.title: Feature: DNS Armor now in preview

entry.content:
DNS64 is available in GA.

DNS64 provides synthesized IPv6 addresses for IPv4 destinations. For more information, see the following:

  • DNS64 overview
  • Configure DNS64 server policies
entry.summary: The DNS64 feature is now generally available, allowing for synthesized IPv6 addresses for IPv4 destinations.
entry.title: Feature: DNS64 now generally available

entry.content: Using a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) forwarding target is available for outbound DNS forwarding in GA.
entry.summary: You can now use a fully qualified domain name for outbound DNS forwarding in Google Cloud. This feature is now generally available.
entry.title: Feature: FQDN Support for Outbound DNS Forwarding
